The request page, end to end

Fifteen steps from an owner who has never heard of this to a stranger asking for a time and being answered — and on to a nicer address, and to what happens when the subscription stops. Every screen carries what it does, why it is that way, and anything still open on it.

Calendar Mirror 2.0 Copy generated from Copy.json Data from review-fixture.json — synthetic Light and dark follow your system
What this is and is not. The words, the order and the reasoning are real — the copy is generated from the same file the app's strings are, so it cannot drift. The rendering is not: this is HTML and the app is SwiftUI, so spacing, type and color come from the simulator, not from here. Nothing in it has been compiled — there is no Swift toolchain in the session that wrote it, and CI is the first real build. Every name, calendar and time below is invented; the live config is never used for this.

Which calendars count

On the device only

Two checkboxes per calendar, in the window the owner already uses to look at their calendars.

Why — Use for requests is exactly one, enforced at the control rather than by a validation message — the Kit writes into a single CalRef.

5

Your day

On the device only

The policy, asked as a sentence that reads aloud, with the zone stated on the line rather than inferred from the device.

Why — maxPerDay and the horizon are privacy controls wearing the clothes of preferences — publishing every free half-hour tells a stranger your week is empty.

Open — Six settings in three groups, each with a one-line footer. The two-and-a-third screens the first run measured came from the captions, not the controls.

8

Apple's sheet, then the page

askwhen.me

StoreKit takes the payment method; the device sends Apple's signed transaction and askwhen.me returns a slug and a write token.

Why — The service verifies Apple's signature itself and derives the entitlement — it never learns a name, an address or a card, and the device never sends a hash it could have made up.

10

Someone asks

askwhen.me

A stranger picks a time, confirms by email, and the device collects it on the next poll. A notification arrives carrying Accept and Decline.

Why — Nothing is pushed to the owner — the service holds no address for them. The device collects, so the notification is not a convenience on top of a feed; it is the arrival.

11

The slot is gone

On the device only

Accept re-checks the calendar first. If something landed since the time was offered, nothing is written and nobody is told.

Why — This is the one thing this architecture does better than a hosted competitor: the device holds the truth, so it notices before writing. A hosted service believes its own copy.

Open — "What landed" is a time, never a title — BusyInterval carries no title by design. Whether the owner should see their own event's name here is your call, and it means a new path through the privacy boundary.
Request conflict

That time is taken

Priya Raman asked for Thursday 24 September, 1:30 PM, and something has landed on it since you offered it. Nothing has been written, and nobody has been told anything yet.

What is on it now
Thursday 24 September — 1:00–2:00 PM

Shown as a time only. This is the same busy/free view the page is built from — the app does not read what your events are called.

Nearest times still open
Thursday 24 September, 3:00 PM
Friday 25 September, 10:00 AM
Friday 25 September, 2:30 PM

Declining tells them the time is gone. There is no way to offer one of these back to them from here — they would have to ask again — so if one of these works, say so when you reply.

Decline

Writes it into your calendar on top of whatever is there. Sometimes that is exactly right — you know what the clash is and this matters more.

12

Claiming an address

askwhen.me

The slug always works. On top of it the owner types either a label for a subdomain of askwhen.me, or a domain they already own.

Why — Whatever is typed is normalized before it is claimed — case folded, trimmed, a pasted URL reduced to its host, a trailing dot dropped. Each of those is a correct answer arriving looking wrong, and each would otherwise claim a hostname that can never verify.

Open — The field is offered only on a tier that includes it; otherwise the same section shows why, and an Upgrade button. That variant is 12b.

13

Waiting for DNS

askwhen.me

A subdomain verifies on arrival and has nothing more to say. A custom domain comes back unverified, carrying the CNAME to set and what DNS answers instead.

Why — Checking is not a refresh button — GET /domains makes the service re-read DNS and issue the certificate the moment the record is right, so asking is what makes it start working. The service’s own diagnosis is shown verbatim, because it knows what DNS answered and the device does not.

Address

dana.askwhen.me ✓ Working

ask.okonkwo-referees.com ◷ Waiting for DNS

Add this record

CNAME ask.okonkwo-referees.com → edge.askwhen.me

What DNS says right now

ask.okonkwo-referees.com. 300 IN A 203.0.113.9

That is an A record pointing somewhere else. Replace it with the CNAME above.

Check now

Checking is what makes it start working — the service re-reads DNS every time you ask, and issues the certificate the moment the record is right.

14

The subscription ends

askwhen.me

Seven days of grace. The page stays up saying “not currently taking requests”, then askwhen.me deletes it and the link 404s.

Why — That line is the same one a page shows when the publisher has been offline a while, so a visitor learns nothing about the owner’s billing. Renewing inside the grace brings the same page back at the same address, which is the fact that decides whether someone renews.

Open — The device counts the grace down, but the service is the authority — it deletes from Apple’s server notifications and this device may have slept through it. Finding the slug gone is what settles it.
Your page

⚠ Your subscription has ended

Your page is still there, but it is not taking requests. Anyone who opens it sees “not currently taking requests” — the same line it shows when your device has been offline for a while, so it does not announce anything about you.

It is deleted in 4 days.

When that happens the page, its address and anything still in its queue are removed, and the link 404s. Your calendar is untouched — every request you already accepted is an ordinary event and stays exactly where it is.

Renewing inside the grace brings the same page back at the same address, so the links you have sent out keep working.

15

It is gone

askwhen.me

The grace ran out. The page, its address and its queue are removed; a new subscription starts a new page at a new address.

Why — The sentence that matters is that the calendar is untouched — every request already accepted is an ordinary event that never depended on the page staying up.

Your page

Your page has been deleted

The grace period ended and AskWhen.me removed the page. Links to the old address no longer work, and there is nothing left to restore — a new subscription starts a new page with a new address.

Everything you accepted is still in your calendar. Nothing that was already agreed depended on the page staying up.
